newsitem.title: UK: Pensions, voting reform dominate UK political day.
newsitem.headline: Pensions, voting reform dominate UK political day.

text.p: Britain's three main parties on Wednesday raised their sights from the coming election to unveil radical pension and electoral proposals that may not win votes but, if implemented, could profoundly change the country.

Prime Minister John Major, fighting to claw back a big deficit in opinion polls, announced plans for what he called a pensions "revolution" aimed at defusing a demographic timebomb that could go off next century as Britain's population ages.
At the same time, the main opposition Labour party and the smaller Liberal Democrats pledged to work together to push through sweeping changes to Britain's patchwork constitution.

There is no evidence either issue is a big preoccupation for Britons, who will vote soon -- probably on May 1 -- whether to re-elect Major's Conservatives for an unprecedented fifth straight term or turn to Labour for the first time since 1979.
The Conservatives' pension reforms would be phased in over a generation, so Major said it was wrong to portray them as designed to sway undecided voters.

Instead, he said, the proposals were an example of Britain stealing a march on its European Union partners and tackle the problems that will arise when an ageing population has to be supported by a shrinking workforce.

"This will put us another huge step ahead -- enabling us to sustain a healthy, low-tax economy for the future," he told a news conference at his Downing Street residence. "It is dealing with the long-term issues in a far-sighted way."
In a nutshell, under Major's complex proposals, every individual would build up a personal savings and investment fund in their own name that would provide an income on retirement.
To feed the account, employees would be given a rebate on part of their national insurance contributions -- a payroll tax used to fund pensions and welfare benefits.
The state would thus no longer have to finance basic pensions, as now, from tax revenues.

This would save taxpayers an estimated 40 billion pounds ($64.5 billion) a year by the middle of next century, although the state would guarantee that everyone received a basic pension in case the individual investment funds performed badly.
The Labour/Liberal Democrat proposals are no less ambitious for they could mean the coming election is the last to be held under the widely criticised first-past-the-post voting system.
Under first-past-the-post, the Conservatives have won overall majorities in four successive general elections without polling more than 44 percent of the vote in any of them.

The two opposition parties said they had agreed to hold a referendum on adopting proportional representation (PR) which, if adopted, would mean that governments with an overall majority in parliament would become the exception rather than the rule.
"This is an historic occasion," said Labour's foreign affairs spokesman, Robin Cook, who led his party in four months of talks with the Liberal Democrats.
"Two political parties who will be competing against each other in the general election have cooperated together to agree on a radical and comprehensive programme of constitutional reform," he said.

The two parties also agreed to co-operate to set up separate parliaments in Scotland and Wales, abolish the right of hereditary peers to sit in the upper House of Lords and bring in Britain's first freedom of information act.
Polls suggest it is Labour leader Tony Blair, not Major, who will get the chance to put his policies into practice.

A Reuter survey released on Wednesday of 20 psephologists and pollsters pointed to a 59-seat Labour majority in the new parliament, up from the panel's average prediction in February of a 48-seat majority, and 43 in January.
